# INTRODUCTION.

---

*Whenever a <term>man of desire<note>original: "homme de desir." A key term in the philosophy of Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin, describing a person who feels a deep, spiritual longing to return to a state of divine grace and seeks to help others do the same.</note></term> feels compelled to make his voice heard by mortals, he cannot help but cry out: O holy truth, what shall I tell them! You have made of me a kind of wretched victim, destined to sigh in vain for their happiness.*

*You have lit within me a searing fire, which corrodes my entire being at once.*

*I feel for the rest of the human family a zeal—or rather, an imperious need—that obsesses me and consumes me.*

*I can neither avoid it nor fight it, so much does it torment and master me.*

*To crown these ills, this unfortunate zeal is reduced to feeding on its own substance, and to devouring itself, for lack of finding a way to satisfy the hunger you have given me for the peace of souls.*

*It ends unceasingly in sobs that stifle the sounds of my voice.*

*It leaves me no respite, except to plunge me, a moment later, into new sorrows, and leave me a prey to new lamentations.*

*And it is in this state that you urge me to raise my voice among my fellow men!!!!!*

<summary>The author describes an overwhelming, almost painful spiritual compulsion to share a "holy truth" with humanity, expressing a deep sense of sacrifice and emotional turmoil.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION.

*Besides, how shall I make myself heard by the <term>men of the torrent<note>original: "hommes du torrent." A metaphorical term for people swept away by the rush of worldly passions, material interests, and the fleeting fashions of the time, leaving them no space for spiritual reflection.</note></term>!*

I have only <term>principles<note>original: "principes." In this mystical context, principles refer to the foundational, unchanging laws of spiritual reality, rather than mere rules of conduct or abstract logic.</note></term> to offer them; and they will answer themselves with opinions, if not with insane illusions, whose glamor will not even let them perceive their own bad faith.

I cannot raise any edifice that does not have as its base their <term>imperishable being<note>A reference to the immortal soul or the divine spark within every human, which the author believes persists despite physical death.</note></term>, all radiant with eternal splendor; and the final limit of their science is to liken themselves to inert and powerless dust.

I would wish, by reviving in them the pride of their title, to animate them with the glorious desire to renew their alliance with the universal unity; and they have armed themselves against this unity, and seem to watch only to erase it from the count of beings.

I would desire, by using only the <term>word of life<note>original: "parole de vie." Likely a reference to the Logos or a spiritualized form of speech that has the power to create and transform, as opposed to empty or mechanical human language.</note></term> with them, to lead them to not employ a single word of their own that was not vivified by that inexhaustible power which vivifies everything; and by dint of having misunderstood this word of life, and having wanted to do without its help, they have transformed all their languages into so many instruments of confusion and death.

But above all, must I not purge myself of my own stains! Must I not solemnly pronounce my divorce from my infidelities! Must I not cleanse and <term>divinize<note>original: "diviniser." To restore or awaken the divine nature within oneself through spiritual purification and alignment with God.</note></term> myself before thinking of cleansing and divinizing others!

*I come to exercise toward man, my fellow, a more truthful and severe ministry; I come to perform the important <term>ministry of man<note>original: "ministère de l'homme." *The happiness that should belong to our species now only appears among us as a rarity and a wonder. Our tears are today the only signs of our brotherhood; we are no longer kin except through misfortune. Such is this fatal rede-*

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

...[objects], your rages or your delusions; or only to deceive and lead others astray through the countless and misleading fictions of your thought?

If a single glance is enough to disillusion you regarding the frivolous and guilty use of your **faculties** <note>original: "facultés." In the context of 18th-century mystical philosophy, these are the inherent spiritual and intellectual powers—such as will, intellect, and imagination—that the author believes were given to humans for a divine purpose.</note>, a single glance should also suffice to disillusion you about the results you gain from them. Weigh all these results in the balance; you will not find one that does not escape you, or that does not fall short of your hopes; that does not feed you with anxieties, or that does not end by costing you tears.

What, then, is this region where nothing that is *ourselves* fulfills its **law** <note>original: "loi." This refers to the "true law" or the natural, divine order that a being is supposed to follow to achieve its purpose.</note>, and where we do not taste a single joy that does not deceive us! Yes, a dominating and seemingly fundamental **illusion** <note>original: "prestige." In the author's time, this word did not mean social status, but rather a magical spell, a deceptive appearance, or a "glamour" that blinds the senses.</note> appears to make up the atmosphere in which we are immersed. We are reduced to constantly and almost exclusively breathing this vapor of illusion that surrounds us, which we then pass on to one another after having further infected it with our own **corruption**; or if we wish to protect ourselves from it, we must condemn ourselves to suspend the activity of *all our faculties* and exist in total immobility.

In the Alps, look at that hunter who is sometimes surprised and suddenly enveloped by a sea of thick vapors, where he cannot even see his own feet or his own hand; and where he is forced to stop exactly where he stands, for lack of being able to take a single step in safety. What this hunter is only by accident and at intervals, man is here below continually and without respite. His earth- <note>The word is cut off and likely continues as "terrestres" (earthly) on the following page.</note>

<summary>The author argues that human life is lived in a "vapor of illusion," where our inherent faculties are misused and our joys are deceptive. He uses the metaphor of an Alpine hunter lost in thick fog to describe the permanent state of spiritual blindness and paralysis that affects humanity.</summary>

*[o]thers are themselves this sea of dark vapors which hide from it the light of its sun, and constrain it to remain in a painful inaction, if it does not wish, at the slightest movement, to break itself and plunge into precipices.* <note>original: "vapeurs ténébreuses." In the mystical tradition of the author, these "dark vapors" represent the sensory and material distractions that cloud the soul’s spiritual perception of divine light.</note>

Men quick to judge, no doubt my writing should not expect a very brilliant success among you. You will not forgive me for believing entirely in a truth, since by dint of teaching doubt, you allow us at most only half-beliefs, not to say that you allow us none at all.

If, however, I had the happiness of doing some *good*, I would easily console myself for making no *noise* <note>original: "bruit." In the 18th century, "making noise" meant achieving public fame, notoriety, or becoming a fashionable topic of conversation.</note>; I would even consider myself amply rewarded and would not complain at all about the sentence of my judges; especially since if they had thought me worthy of being enlisted under their banners, I would also have had to take a side for the opinions that dominate them, and for the principles they profess; now, I could not have served for long under such standards.

Moreover, if I must renounce the **incense** <note>original: "l’encens." A metaphor for the flattering praise and adulation of the public.</note> of the many, my cause will not be lost because of it, because it has the right to be brought before a fixed and competent tribunal, whose judgments are not exposed to the fluctuations of human opinions.

Perhaps even the time is not far off when Europeans will eagerly cast their eyes upon objects that the majority among them view only with distrust, and even with contempt. Their **scientific edifice** <note>original: "édifice scientifique." The author is likely referring to the strictly materialist and rationalist science of the Enlightenment, which he views as having a fragile or incomplete foundation because it ignores spiritual origins.</note> is not solid enough

<summary>The author anticipates criticism from skeptical intellectuals who promote doubt, stating he prefers quiet spiritual utility over public fame. *...find these same dogmas spread across such distant places and at such remote eras from one another.*

*While I wait to become better acquainted with these theosophical <term>theosophical: relating to "theosophy," a system of philosophy or religion that proposes to establish direct contact with the divine through mystical insight or spiritual intuition.</term> riches of Asia, and to draw useful enlightenment from them myself, I must caution that they can no more than other books carry man beyond speculative spiritualism <note>speculative spiritualism: an intellectual or theoretical belief in the soul or spiritual matters, which the author considers a mere first step.</note>; it is only the radical development of our inner essence that can lead us to active spiritualism <note>active spiritualism: a lived, practical experience of spiritual power and direct union with the divine, characterized by internal transformation rather than just study.</note>.*

*It is also upon this indispensable foundation that the work I publish today rests, as well as all those I have published previously.*

*Descartes rendered an essential service to the natural sciences by applying algebra to material geometry. I do not know if I shall have rendered as great a service to thought by applying man—as I have done in all my writings—to that species of living and divine geometry which encompasses everything, and of which I regard the Man-as-Spirit <note>original: "l'Homme-Esprit." A central concept in Saint-Martin's philosophy, referring to the human being restored to their original spiritual dignity and function as a mediator between God and the universe.</note> as being the true algebra and the universal analytical instrument; this would be a satisfaction for me that I would not dare hope for, even if I allowed myself to desire it. But such a comparison with that famous geometer, in the employment of our faculties, would be one more similarity to add to those he and I already share in a less important order, among which I shall mention only one: that we were both born in that beautiful region known as the garden of France <note>original: "le jardin de la France." This refers to the province of Touraine, the birthplace of both René Descartes (born in La Haye en Touraine) and the author, Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin (born in Amboise).</note>.*

## FIRST PART.

### *On Nature.*

---

Human intelligence, by dint of focusing only on things of the external order—of which it cannot even manage to give a satisfying account of itself—shuts itself off even more from the nature of its own being than from that of the visible objects surrounding it; and yet, as soon as man ceases for a moment to observe the true character of his inward essence <note>original: "essence intime." This refers to the soul's deep, spiritual reality</note>, he quickly becomes entirely blind to the eternal divine source from which he descends. For if man, restored to his primitive elements <note>The fundamental spiritual components that make up the human soul in its original state</note>, is the witness *par excellence* and the positive sign by which this supreme and universal source can be known, that source must fade from our minds as soon as we remove the true mirror that has the property of reflecting it back to us.

When, subsequently, praiseworthy writers and estimable defenders of the truth wish to try to prove that there is a God, and to deduce from His existence all the resulting consequences, no longer finding this

It would therefore already be a great glory for our species, just as it would be a great wisdom in Providence, for all the proofs taken from the order of this world to be so defective. It is not even very difficult to agree that it is by a misuse of language that we call the world where we are not "the other world," and that it is this world which truly is the *other world* for us.

For if, strictly speaking, two things can be "other" respectively to one another, there is nevertheless between them a priority, whether of fact or of convention, which obliges us to regard the second as "other" in relation to the first, and not the first as "other" in relation to the second; since that which is first is *one* and can offer no difference, having no point of comparison prior to itself; whereas that which is second finds this point of comparison before it.

Such is the case with the two worlds in question. The pure spirits <note>In Saint-Martin's cosmology, these are unfallen celestial beings.</note> feel indeed that they are in the other world, and they feel it perpetually and without interruption, because they live only by the life of this other world; but they feel that they are only the inhabitants of this other life, and that another than themselves is its owner.

Man, although being in this terrestrial world, is indeed always in that other world which is everything; but sometimes he feels its sweet influence, sometimes he does not feel it; often even he feels and follows only the impulse of the mixed and dark world <note>The "mixed world" refers to the physical universe where good and evil, spirit and matter, are temporarily intertwined.</note> which is as if coagulated in the midst of this other world, and which is, in relation to that other world, like a wound, a wen, or an <term>abscess</term> <note>Original: "apostume." What idea should we then form of this nature, or of this universe which makes us so blind to that other world, or to that spiritual world—whether good or evil—from which we never depart? We can know it in two words.

Without the evil spiritual world, nature would be an eternal duration of regularity and perfection; without the good spiritual world, nature would be an eternal duration of abomination and disorder. It is the supreme wisdom or love which, to temper the false eternity <note>The "false eternity" refers to the hellish state or the realm of fallen spirits who exist outside of God's light but are trapped in their own permanence.</note>, has judged it appropriate to oppose it with a ray of the true eternity. The mixture of these two eternities composes time, which is neither one nor the other, and which nevertheless offers a successive image of both, through good and evil, through day and night, life and death, etc.

Supreme love could only employ for this work powers descended from the true eternity; and this is why, on one hand, everything is measured in time; and on the other, why time, whether general or particular, must necessarily pass.

# THE MINISTRY

But as the **true eternity** has, so to speak, come out of itself to contain the **false eternity**, and as, on the contrary, the **false eternity** was thereby forced to retreat; this is why we have so much trouble recognizing these two eternities within time, for neither of them is in its proper place there. This is why it is so difficult to prove the **complete God** <note>In Saint-Martin’s thought, the "complete God" represents the fullness of the divine unity, which is obscured in the material world because nature is "fragmented" and "mixed" with opposing forces.</note> through this nature where everything is fragmented and mixed, and where the two eternities only show themselves under the external veil of corruptible matter.

In the state of apathy into which man plunges himself through his own daily illusions, and through his studies applied solely to the external order of nature, he sees in her neither the source of her apparent regularity, nor the hidden source of her disorder. He identifies himself with this external universe; he cannot help but take it for a world, and even for an exclusive and sole existing world.

Also, in this state of affairs, the idea that has the most difficulty finding access to man is that of the <term>degradation</term> <note>Specifically, the "Fall of Man" from a higher spiritual state into the material world.</note> of our species, as well as the alteration of nature itself in which he finds himself placed, and over which the rights he was meant to exercise no longer concern him, because he has allowed them to fall into disuse. He has ended up confusing this blind and dark nature with himself and with his own essence.

However, if he wished to consider the <term>external order</term> <note>The physical, material universe perceived by the senses.</note> for a moment from a truer and more profitable perspective, a simple observation would serve to make him see at once the actual degradation of his species, the dignity of his being, and his superiority over the external order.

# ON THE SPIRIT-MAN.

Could men deny the **degradation** <note>The "Fall," or the descent of the human soul from a divine state into the physical world.</note> of their species, when they see that they cannot exist, live, act, or think, except by struggling against a resistance? Our blood must defend itself against the resistance of the elements; our spirit, against that of doubt and the darkness of ignorance; our heart, against that of false inclinations; our entire body, against that of inertia; our social acts, against that of disorder, and so on.

A resistance is an obstacle; an obstacle in the realm of the spirit is an antipathy and an enmity; but an enmity in action is a hostile and combating power. Now, this power, by constantly extending its forces around us, keeps us in a violent and painful situation in which we ought not to be, and outside of which this power would be to us as if unknown and as if non-existent, since we feel internally that we are made for peace and rest.

No, man is not within the measures proper to him; he is evidently in a state of **alteration** <note>In this context, "alteration" refers to a corruption or change from an original, perfect form.</note>. It is not because this proposition is in books that I say this of him; it is not because this idea is widespread among all peoples; it is because man seeks this place of rest for his spirit everywhere; it is because he wants to conquer all sciences, even that of the <term>infinite</term> <note>The "infinite" here refers to the divine source or the totality of spiritual truth, which Saint-Martin believes is man's natural intellectual home.</note>, even though it constantly escapes him, and because he would rather disfigure it and accommodate it to his dark conceptions than do without it; it is because, during his fleeting existence on this earth, he seems to be in the midst of his fellow men only like a voracious lion among sheep, or like a sheep among lions.

Astral and terrestrial nature operates the <term>laws of creation</term> <note>In the author's system, these are the divine principles that govern the formation and movement of both the physical and spiritual worlds.</note>, and was born and exists only through the inherent power of these laws.

The vegetable and the mineral possess the *effect* of these laws, for they contain the properties of all elementary, astral, and other essences, and this with more efficacy and development than the stars themselves, which contain only half of these properties, and the earth which contains only the other half.

The animal has the *use* of these laws of creation, since it is charged with nourishing, reproducing, and maintaining itself, and because within it reside all the principles necessary to contribute to the maintenance of its existence.

# OF THE SPIRIT-MAN

As for all these material rights that man possesses and which we have concluded with the baker’s handling, if we transport ourselves in thought into the real region of man, we will undoubtedly sense that all these rights can be justified in a way that is even more vast and more <term>virtual</term> <note>In this context, "virtual" (from the Latin *virtus*) refers to inherent spiritual power, potency, or efficacy rather than something simulated.</note> still, by probing and discovering the marvelous properties that constitute the **Spirit-Man**, and what high handlings can arise from them.

For if man so obviously has the power to be a worker and a handler of earthly productions, why could he not also be a worker and a handler of productions of a higher order? He must be able to compare these divine productions with their source, just as he has the power to compare the total effect of nature with the cause that formed and directs it, and he is the only one who possesses this privilege.

Nevertheless, experience alone can give the idea of this sublime right, and even this very idea must constantly appear new to the one who is most accustomed to it.

But alas! man knows his spiritual rights, and he does not enjoy them! Does he need any other proof to attest to his deprivation, and consequently his **degradation**?

# THE MINISTRY

Man, open your eyes for a moment; for with your inconsistent judgments, not only will you not recover your privileges, but you will be even less able to eliminate them. Even physical beings do not cease to give you lessons that ought to instruct you. Animals are all heart; and it is quite clear that although they are not machines <note>A rebuttal of the "animal-machine" theory proposed by René Descartes, which argued animals had no souls or feelings.</note>, they nevertheless have no spirit, since it is, as it were, distinct from them, outside of them, and alongside them. For this reason, they do not have to establish, as we do, a **covenant** <note>original: "alliance," which can mean alliance, marriage, or a biblical covenant</note> between themselves and their **principle** <term>Principle</term> <note>In this philosophical context, "Principle" (principe) refers to the divine source or the foundational spiritual origin of a being.</note>. But seeing the regularity of their path, one cannot deny, to the shame of man, that the collective of non-free beings <note>Referring to animals and nature, which act by instinct/necessity rather than free will.</note> manifests a more continuous and more complete covenant than that which we are masters of forming within ourselves with our principle. One could even go so far as to say that, except for man, the universality of beings appears to us as so many hearts of which God is the spirit.

Indeed, the world or the strayed man wants to be all spirit, and believes he can do without his true heart, or his sacred and divine heart, provided that he puts forward his animal heart and his pride.

In God, there is also a sacred heart and a spirit, since we are his image; but they are one, like all the faculties and powers of this sovereign being.

Now, our rights can go as far as forming, like the supreme wisdom, an eternal and indissoluble covenant between our spirit and our sacred heart, by uniting them in the principle that formed them; and it will only be upon this indispensable condition that we can hope to return ourselves anew...

...of our immortality, it would be to observe that in every respect, man walks daily here below beside his grave, and that it can only be through some inherent sense of his immortality that, in all these cases, he seeks to show himself superior to this danger.

This is what can be said of warriors, who at any moment may receive a death blow. It is also what can be said of the corporeal man, who indeed can at any instant be withdrawn from this world: there is no other difference except that the warrior is not necessarily the victim of this danger, and many escape it; whereas natural men all succumb to it, without it being possible for them to protect themselves from it.

But there is in these two classes the same tranquility, not to say the same carelessness <gloss>carelessness: *insouciance*</gloss>, which causes the warrior and the natural man to live as if the danger did not exist for them. That is to say, their very carelessness is an indication that they are, as it were, filled with the idea of their immortality, even though both walk on the edge of their grave.

From a spiritual perspective, the danger for man is even greater, and his carelessness is even more extreme; not only does the **man-spirit** <term>Man-Spirit (*L'homme-esprit*): Saint-Martin’s term for the human being restored to their divine function. In Martinist thought, "lies" or "falsehood" refers to the illusory nature of the material world and the deceptive influence of spiritual evil.</note>; but are there not even many among the human race who already walk continually *within* their grave? And yet, the blind man does not even occupy himself with the means of getting out, nor does he inquire if he will ever emerge!

### THE MINISTRY

When he has the good fortune to perceive for a single moment that he walks in this pit <note>original: "fosse." This can mean a pit, a trench, or a grave. In Saint-Martin’s mystical context, it refers to the spiritual abyss of the material world.</note>, it is then that he has a truly irresistible spiritual proof of his immortality; for he has the spiritual proof of his dreadful *mortality*, and even of what we figuratively call his *death*. Now, how could he feel the torment and the horror of his spiritual mortality, if he did not at the same time have the energetic sense of his immortality?

It is only in this contrast that his suffering is found; just as physical pains are only felt through the opposition of disorder and derangement against health. But this kind of proof likewise can only be acquired through experience, and it is one of the first fruits of the work of regeneration <term>regeneration: *régénération*. In Martinist philosophy, this is the process of the "New Man" being reborn and returning to his original divine state through spiritual labor.</term>; for if we do not feel our *spiritual death*, how can we think to call upon *life*?

It is also there that we learn once more that there is an even more unhappy being, undoubtedly; that is the prince of lies <note>original: "prince du mensonge." This refers to the source of evil or the Devil, who lacks the "ray of light" necessary to even realize his own wretched state.</note>, since without him we would not even have an idea of him, given that each thing can only be revealed by itself, as could be seen in *The Spirit of Things* <note>Saint-Martin is referring to his own published work, *De l’Esprit des choses* (1800), which explores the inner nature of existence.</note>.

Not only does he walk incessantly in his pit, not only does he never perceive that he walks in this pit, since he would need for that the help of a ray of light; but as we approach this pit, we feel that he is in a continual dissolution and corruption, that is to say, he is perpetually in the proof and the effective feeling of his *death*; that he never conceives the slightest hope—

I have the right to suppose here that all these facts are accepted; it is no longer a matter of proving them, but of learning how to make use of them. What are all these writers who seek only to make us contributors to their noisy and vain fame, instead of sacrificing themselves for our true utility? What are all these false friends of man, who are quite willing to speak to him of **virtue** and **truth**, but who take great care to leave him in peace in inaction and lies, so much do they fear that if they sought to tear him away from them by their austere words, he would withdraw from their school, and thereby put a

Man! Man! Leave aside those books so fruitless for you, and throw yourself into the path of **works**, if you are happy enough to understand the true meaning of this word. This is what ensures that the books of the true **administrators** of the **divine thing** <term>chose divine: a term used by Saint-Martin to refer to the active, sacred reality of the spiritual world.</term> offer at all times to the **man of desire** <term>homme de desir: a central concept in this philosophy, referring to the person who actively yearns for spiritual truth and reintegration with the Divine.</term>, a spirit of life always ready to quench the thirst he has for truth; they are like those beautiful roads that serve as communication between great cities, and which offer at once interesting vistas, beneficial shelters, and even vigilant defenders against dangers and ill-intentioned people. They are like those cheerful and fertile hills, placed by the hand of nature along the rivers that fertilize them, and to which they provide, in their turn, useful boundaries so that the navigator may make upon their waves a journey as peaceful as it is enchanting.

Thus, all men of God are accountable to the world for all their thoughts. For if they are truly men of God, none comes to them that does not have as its goal the **perfection** of things and the extension of the **reign of the Master**.

As much, therefore, as he who is not an administrator of divine things must distrust his thoughts and spare other men the knowledge of them; so much...

What am I saying, the intelligence of man? Could it even be opened with the most perfect of books? It has degraded itself, it has obscured itself, it has likened itself to that of childhood. ...universal and eternal harmony which has led, in all times, famous men to regard the current state of nature as being eternal, despite the evils and the disorders in which it is plunged.

Yes, everything is eternal in the fundamental bases of things, but not in the pain and in this horrible confusion that show themselves in every part of nature: yes, there is undoubtedly an **eternal nature** <note>In Saint-Martin’s philosophy, "eternal nature" refers to the divine, unfallen state of the universe, as opposed to the "temporal nature" we currently inhabit.</note>, where everything is more regular, more active, and more alive than in this one where we are imprisoned; and the strongest proof that the current nature where we are imprisoned is not eternal, is that it suffers and that it is the dwelling place of death in every form, while only life is eternal.

Therefore, I am quite willing to agree: you teach me great and useful doctrines, you, estimable writers, who, by your precepts, lead man back to **brotherly charity**, to zeal for the **house of God**, and to the care of emerging from this **earthly mire** <note>original: "fange terrestre," a metaphor for the physical or corrupted world</note>, without having been defiled by its infection.

For me, I feel that they still lack something to fill the **immensity of desires** that devour me. The prayers and the truths that are given and taught to us here below are too small for us; they are only the **truths of time**: we feel that we are made for something else.

I conceive that brotherly charity seems to have nothing more sublime to practice than to forgive our enemies, and to do good to those who hate us.

Man did not begin his wanderings <note>original: "écarts." Instead, he began his wanderings through weakness, as all his children still do today in their infancy, where objects of ambition do not move them; and this weakness consisted in having allowed himself to be struck, attracted, and penetrated by the spirit of the universe, while the wretched man belonged to an order and a region above the region of this world.

When he had descended to this inferior level, the enemy had every advantage to foster within him the ideas of ambition which he would not have had otherwise, and without anyone speaking to him of those objects of ambition which were unknown to him. As soon as we notice that the universe has no word <note>original: "parole". For Saint-Martin, "the Word" is the divine, creative power. ...the power to retain it, and then this **vessel** <note>original: "matras." A long-necked glass flask used in chemistry and alchemy. Here, the author uses it as a metaphor for the material container or substrate of a being.</note> falls back into its minimum, not to say into its nothingness, since it no longer has **spirituous** <note>original: "spiritueuses." Refers to active, refined energies that act as a bridge between the purely spiritual and the physical.</note> bases to reactivate it.

Thus, first, matter is not divisible to infinity when considering it in terms of the divisibility of its substance—an operation that we have demonstrated elsewhere cannot even begin, as seen in **organic bodies** which cannot be divided without perishing; second, it is not even divisible to infinity in each of its particular actions, since each of these particular actions ceases as soon as the **spirituous** base that serves as its subject is withdrawn; thus, the limit of this action is the retreat and disappearance of this same base.

Regarding this divisibility, considered abstractly and within our thought, it has even less possibility, since it is only our own conception that serves as a base for this pretended matter that we continually forge for ourselves; and indeed, as long as our spirit presents to matter such a **substratum** <note>original Latin: "substratum." Literally "that which is spread under"; the underlying foundation or substance of a thing.</note> or such a germ, this matter takes hold of it in our thought and serves as its form and envelope.

Thus, as long as we dwell on this divisibility, or conceive of its sensible results, we find this divisibility possible and real, since the sensible form always follows the base that we offer it; but as soon as we turn the eyes of our spirit away from this focus of action, which we only approach intellectually, this form disappears, and there is no longer for it, nor for us, any divisibility of matter.

If the learned ancients and moderns, from the **Platos** and **Aristotles** to the **Newtons** and **Spinozas**, had known how to pay attention to the fact that matter is only a representation and an image of what it is not, they would not have tormented themselves so much, nor gone so far astray in wanting to tell us what it was.

It is like the portrait of an <note>Possibly a printer's error for "une"</note> absent person; one must absolutely know the model to be able to ensure the resemblance. Without this, the portrait will be nothing more for us than a work of fantasy, upon which everyone will make whatever conjectures they please, without any assurance that any of them are true.

Nevertheless, in this series of the formation of beings which has just occupied us, there is an important point that resists our knowledge; it is the **magism** <note>original: "magisme." For Saint-Martin, this refers to the active, generative power or the "magic" of the divine will that brings things into being.</note> of the generation of things, and yet it only resists us because we seek to reach, through analysis, what is in itself only graspable by a hidden impression; one might even say that on this point **Jacob Boehme** <note>A 17th-century German mystic who deeply influenced Saint-Martin; known for his complex cosmology.</note> has lifted almost all the veils by revealing to our spirit the <term>seven forms of nature</term> <note>Boehme's system describing the seven qualities or stages through which the divine will manifests as a physical and spiritual reality.</note>, even unto the eternal root of beings.

The true character of *magism* is to be the medium and the means of passage from the state of absolute dispersion or indifference—which Boehme calls **abyssal** <note>original: "abyssale." Derived from Boehme's "Ungrund," the bottomless, undifferentiated void or primordial will that exists before manifest nature.</note>—to any state of characterized **sensitization** <note>original: "sensibilisation." The process by which something becomes perceptible to the senses or takes on a distinct, formal existence.</note>, whether spiritual or natural, whether simple or elementary.

The generation, or this passage from the insensible state to the sensible state, is perpetual. It holds the middle ground between the dispersed and insensible state of things and their state of characterized sensitization; and yet it is neither one nor the other, since it is neither the dispersion like—

But, he asks himself, how did it determine the motions of revolution and rotation of the planets? He answers: that if these bodies had penetrated this fluid, its resistance would have caused them to fall into the sun; thus one can conjecture that they were formed at the successive limits of this atmosphere, by the condensation of zones which it must have abandoned in the plane of its equator, while cooling and condensing upon the surface of this star... one can further conjecture that the satellites <note>In the language of the time, "satellites" refers to moons orbiting planets.</note> were formed in a similar manner, by the atmospheres of the planets; finally, that the five phenomena <note>Laplace identified five specific regularities in the solar system, such as all planets moving in the same direction and in roughly the same plane, which his theory sought to explain.</note> he previously set forth flow naturally from these hypotheses.

Without further examining these faulty hypotheses, I will say that, in general, what harms the accuracy and truth of the hypotheses birthed by the human spirit is the secret inclination that drives it to seek a uniform mechanism and a single element for the phenomena of nature, as these seem to it to be the most regular and the most perfect.

In terms of explanations, the most perfect is the one that is the most true, however numerous and complicated the causes may be that this explanation tries to account for. Forgetting this truth, it can be said, is what has delayed the development of our knowledge in every field; there is not a single science that has not suffered—and perhaps does not still suffer every day—a noticeable prejudice because of it.

...transmit them, which are easier to grasp than the causes that direct and constitute these organs themselves; because as one penetrates beneath the surface of beings, their faculties become more pronounced and consequently offer more diversity and opposition.

It is thus that to determine the path and the periods that the hands of a watch trace upon its dial, it is enough to observe them with the eyes and follow their monotonous movements; because, as there is only a single fact present, one needs only a single formula to describe and explain it.

If one wishes to penetrate into the interior of the watch, one will find several diverse agents <term>agents: in 18th-century natural philosophy, "agents" refers to the active forces or components that produce a specific effect within a system.</term> there, whose laws will necessarily be more numerous and the explanation less simple than that of the movement of the hands, since there is a sort of combat and opposition between them.

If one wishes to go even further and scrutinize what sets all the wheels of this watch in motion—to calculate the sum of movement, and the sum of the force and resistance that govern all these agents, and to decompose the various substances employed in this mechanism to judge which can best fulfill its purpose—one will see how much the branches of science will multiply. One would then see how far from the truth they would be if they wished to embrace these different branches within a single law, and subject them to a single explanation.

### OF THE MAN-SPIRIT.

...so admirable in our modern centuries, and to those magnificent axioms, by means of which, using the simplest laws, he has described the true path of the celestial bodies.

But in this, he has only occupied himself with the face of the watch; and instead of having given us what the learned call the true system of the world <note>The "System of the World" (*systême du monde*) was a standard term in 18th-century astronomy, most notably used by Pierre-Simon Laplace, to describe the mechanical laws governing the universe.</note>, he has in reality only given us the itinerary; and even in this itinerary, he has forgotten what is most essential in any journey, which would be to tell us where the traveler departed from and where he is going.

Thus, when—after having described the movements of the celestial bodies—man has tried to describe their organic and primitive mobility, that is to say, to penetrate into the interior of the watch, we see by the two hypotheses mentioned above how many difficulties he has encountered and how far he has remained behind.

These difficulties have multiplied even further for him when, not content with scrutinizing the organic and primitive mobility of the celestial bodies, he has wished to account for the original formation of these celestial bodies themselves; and the two hypotheses in question can serve as our testimony.

I do not fear to repeat the reason for this; it is because as we penetrate beyond the surface of the operations of nature, various movers <term>movers (mobiles): the active, underlying forces or spiritual principles that trigger movement, as opposed to the mechanical motion itself.</term> characterize themselves, assert themselves, and, by refusing a unity of law as they refuse a unity of action, they consequently refuse any general explanation applicable to the monotony and uniformity of external phenomena, which are but servile results.

He claims that when their anguished fermentation reached the highest degree in this place through the force of heat, then that light of eternal wisdom, which he calls love, or **SOPHIA** <note>original: "SOPHIE"</note>, pierced through the separating barrier and came to balance the heat; because in that instant, the brilliant light rose within what he calls the power of water, or the oiliness of water <term>oiliness of water: a theosophical term for the spiritual substance that acts as the "fuel" or "body" for the divine light to manifest.</term>, and lit the heart of water, which rendered it temperate and restorative.

I stated in *The Spirit of Things* <note>original: "l’esprit des choses." We can hardly refrain from believing that, independently of the earthly fruits that the earth lavishes upon us every day, it still has other fruits to produce. The first of the indications we have of this is seeing the difference between the wild fruits that the earth bears naturally and those we cause it to produce through our cultivation; this might suggest to <term>penetrating eyes: Those capable of seeing beyond the physical surface of things into their spiritual essence.</term> penetrating eyes that the earth is only waiting for the help of man to bring forth even more interesting wonders from its bosom.

### *Of Man.*

To understand the sublimity of our rights, we must trace back to our origin. But before considering the nature of the <term>Man-Spirit</term> <note>original: "l'Homme-Esprit." Saint-Martin uses this term to describe the human being who has regained their original spiritual status and divine function.</note>, we will observe what may generally be called "Spirit," in whatever form it may take; we will lay out the radical sources from which this expression derives, and we will first take this word "spirit" in the various senses under which it can be viewed in our languages.

We can regard the spirit of a thing as being the actual <term>generation</term> <note>original: "engendrement." This suggests a dynamic process where internal powers are birthed or brought into active existence.</note>, whether partial or complete, of the powers belonging to its own order.

It is in this way that music only makes us know what it is through the actual emission of sounds by which it is transmitted to our ears, and which are but the effective expression or the active spirit of the plans or the pictures it wishes to paint for us.

It is in this way that the wind is the actual emission of air compressed by clouds or the powers of the atmos-

Thus, it is the role of this universal spirit to make that unity known to us, and to retrace it for us in its entirety, just as Man temporally retraces for us all the properties of his father and mother, of whom he is the complete and living image.

Yes, by fixing the gaze of our <term>understanding</term> <note>The "understanding" (French: *entendement*) refers to the higher cognitive faculty capable of perceiving spiritual truths.</note> upon this actual and perpetual fruit of eternal unity, we sense that since the powers of this eternal unity are perpetually in a necessary and exclusive dependence upon themselves, and since the fruit of their union is an <term>engendering</term> <note>Original: *engendrement*. A technical term in theosophy for the process by which the Divine brings forth life or consciousness from within itself.</note> that is actual and without end or limit, this fruit must truly be the actual and complete expression of their mutual union. It must contain within itself—and must currently and universally depict—everything that can serve as the foundation for the mutual attraction of these powers for one another.

If the powers of eternal unity are necessarily one in their <term>engendering</term> <note>Original: *engendrement*. This refers to the eternal process by which the Divine expresses its nature through a manifest spirit.</note>, if the **Universal Being**—or the fruit which proceeds from their engendering—also necessarily makes one with them, this is undoubtedly a fundamental reason why its generation is hidden from us, since we cannot consider it separate from its generating sources.

For not only do the generating powers in these partial generations also follow the law of a unity according to their class, but their fruit also makes but one with them, after the likeness of the universal unity. This is true at least in its root and in the **generating act**, even though this fruit afterwards detaches itself from its generating sources, as it belongs to the region of that which is <term>successive</term> <note>Original: *successif*. Who would fear to pause here to contemplate what an admirable thing it is—and one that inspires a kind of religious respect—this profound law by which the origin of everything produced is hidden and unknown even to those who receive that origin!

->### OF THE MAN OF SPIRIT.<-
<note>Original title: *De l'Homme-Esprit*. This is also the title of Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin's 1802 work, exploring the restoration of man’s spiritual faculties.</note>

L

Animals and the other beings of nature also possess a **desire**, but the **will** that crowns this desire is totally foreign to them and separate from them; this is why they do not have to pray, as man does, and why they have only to act.

But it is not only in the source of **admiration** <note>In the 18th-century context, "admiration" refers to a sense of "wonder" or "awe" triggered by the encounter with the Divine.</note>, and in the source of desire and will that man has drawn his origin; it is also in the source of **light**, and consequently this light also formed for him one of the bases of the **divine contract** <note>Original: *contrat divin*. This refers to the primordial covenant or ontological relationship established between God and humanity at the moment of creation.</note>.

This is why man is the first term of the relationships found between himself and all the natural and spiritual objects that surround him. This is why, if he does not know how to account for his own **existence**, he will never account for the existence of any other produced and emanated being.

Indeed, if he has drawn his **origin** from the real source of admiration, desire, will, and light—in a word, from the source of reality—he becomes, in his quality as a real being, the yardstick for all objects and all beings that approach him. It is only by their differences from him that he can measure their existence, their laws, and their action: a profound and important truth, which many people seem to distrust, but which they reject only out of laziness, even when they believe they reject it only out of modesty.

Furthermore, this truth is proven by the daily experience of what occurs among men. For how do men become judges and arbiters in the sciences, in the laws, in the military art, in all their institutions, and in all the arts, finally—

Man is a being charged with continuing God where God no longer makes Himself known by Himself. He does not continue God in His fundamental and divine order <note>Original: *ordre radical*. ...ministry of the law. From the ministry of the law, she <note>Likely referring to "Wisdom" or "Providence," which are feminine nouns in French.</note> made him pass under the ministry of prayer, or the law of grace, which could have restored everything for him.

But since the human priesthood has defiled this path, or rendered it null, it must be suspended in its turn, and active and violent action must replace it, just as prayer or the law of grace replaced the law which the Jews had abused; and it is in this spirit of wisdom, always beneficent, that supreme love directs or allows all these lamentable events to occur, about which terrestrial man murmurs, forgetting that it is his own crimes that cause them, and which overturn the earth, while he was born to pacify and improve everything.

The French Revolution likely had as its object, on the part of Providence, to prune, if not to suspend, this <term>ministry of prayer</term> <note>For Saint-Martin, this represents the Christian era or the institutional Church, which he believed had become stagnant or corrupt, necessitating a "pruning" through the upheavals of the Revolution.</note>, just as the ministry of prayer, at its origin, had the object of suspending the ministry of the Jewish law.

In this regard, the French could be regarded as the people of the new law, just as the Hebrews were the people of the ancient law. One should not be surprised by this election, despite our crimes and our robberies. The Jews who were chosen in their time were no better than the French.

There is, moreover, a factual connection that can be noted; it is that the temple of Jerusalem was destroyed and burned twice, once by Nebuchadnezzar, the other by Titus; and that the days when these two events occurred were the same as the one on which the temporal sceptre of France was broken; that is to say, the 10th of August. <note>August 10, 1792, marked the effective end of the French monarchy when the Tuileries Palace was stormed. Saint-Martin sees a mystical synchronicity between this date and the dates of the destruction of the First and Second Temples (the 9th or 10th of the month of Av in the Hebrew calendar).</note> (See Flavius Josephus, <note>Original: *Flavius Joseph*. A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian whose works were essential for historical-spiritual parallels.</note> *War of the Romans*, Book 6.)

...the work <note>original: *l'œuvre*. In Saint-Martin's thought, this refers to the "Great Work" of spiritual reintegration or the specific "ministry" a person is called to perform for the Divine.</note>, it happens that although storms and tempests might torment us to delay this work, the fountain of life ends up finding this door in those who are fit to be **employed**, and the glory of God triumphs in them to their great satisfaction.

Although God opens this door in those who are employed, those who might not have an employment must not rely on a presumed impossibility, as if no door would open within them; because in all men there is a door for **desire** and for **justice**; and this door, we are all obliged to open ourselves, and we can do so if we are **persevering**.

Regarding the other door, which relates only to the work, it is right that God alone can open it; but also, this door proves nothing for our advancement if the other remains closed by our **indolence** and our **laziness**. One can drive out demons in His name, and yet not be known by Him. <note>A reference to Matthew 7:22-23: "Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils?... As for the reason why things acquired through external ways have such difficulty being truly useful to us, it is because they clash with those that should enter and exit through our true door. It is like a **grafted plant** whose juices fight against the **sap** of the tree upon which the graft is placed; and this struggle lasts until the sap of the tree upon which the graft is placed has taken its natural direction, and carries the new juices along in its course. But also, sometimes it is the sap of the **wild stock** <note>original: *sauvageon*. In botany, the hardy, original plant onto which a more refined branch is grafted.</note> that prevails.

What is the true sap that must carry everything along in its course? You are not ignorant of it, O you who aspire...

...so far removed in its infancy, <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "and if intelligent eyes... concurred with [this progression, they would see the child] so far removed..."</note> that one must collect oneself simply to believe that one day it could be capable of it.

It is that, unfortunately, wisdom—which in itself was formerly intended to provide us with so much joy—must here below clothe itself for us in the garments of mourning and sadness. Today, we must apply our wisdom to suffering instead of rejoicing, because crime <note>original: *le crime*. In the context of Saint-Martin’s writing, this refers to the "Original Fault" or the Fall of Man, which disrupted the natural order.</note> has divided everything and caused there to be two wisdoms. This second or latter wisdom is not life itself, but it gathers life within us, and thereby puts us in a state to receive the primitive wisdom—the source of all joy. Furthermore, it is this sublime primitive wisdom that sustains everything and creates everything. That is why it is forever young.

It would be good to teach the child and encourage them to convince themselves, through their own experience, that prayer must be a continuous spiritual alliance; for we should only pray with God, and our prayer only deserves that name insofar as God prays within us, since it is only in this way that one prays in the kingdom of God.

### THE MINISTRY

It would be good to teach him that doctors are supposed to know all the properties and the nature of the medicinal substances they use for the healing of diseases; that they are supposed to have penetrated all the virtues of remedies, and consequently be in a position to be able to heal all ills. It would be good to show him, according to this, what a shameful degradation this man has undergone.

It would be good to tell him that the man of truth <note>The "man of truth" (*l'homme de vérité*) is Saint-Martin's term for the spiritual seeker who has dedicated themselves to the path of reintegration and divine service.</note> must not enter into relationships with the men of the torrent <term>men of the torrent: a metaphorical term for the worldly masses who are swept away by the current of material desires, public opinion, and superficial concerns</term>, for he would lose too much in the confrontation, and besides, what he exposes to loss is not his own, but his master’s.

# OF THE SPIRIT-MAN #

Yes, human soul, it is surely thus that supreme love has behaved toward you, when it saw that the great scourges of nature—which you had provoked by your oversights—had not made you any wiser. It approached you with all the features of a restless zeal, and by taking a threatening tone, it reminded you of those ancient ordinances upon which your origin and the **divine contract** <term>divine contract: the original spiritual agreement or ontological bond between the Creator and the human soul</term> were founded; which it had pronounced before you after having given you existence; which it had caused to be pronounced again to nature, after you had subjected yourself to its **figurative regime** <term>figurative regime: the material world, which the author views as a symbolic or "representative" state rather than the ultimate reality</term>, and which could at any moment resound within your most intimate being, since you are always originally the organ of the eternal divine source, and since what that source has once pronounced can no longer cease to be pronounced, without interruption, throughout the duration of all eternities.

Thus, let us no longer doubt that all the traditions of peoples offer us traces of this attentive path of supreme love toward you. Let us no longer doubt that since the origin of things, it has conducted itself toward nations as it still does every day toward individuals, striving through violent secret movements to awaken them in the midst of their slumbering states, and to tear them away from the dangers to which they have exposed themselves through their imprudence. Let us not doubt, finally, that it is in this spirit, and by this spirit, that Moses depicted for us in Exodus the supreme voice uttering—amidst lightning and thunder, before the Hebrew people—that imperious and exclusive divine ordinance which the nations had so greatly forgotten: *You shall have no other God before me.* <note>original: "Vous n’aurez point d’autre Dieu devant moi." This refers to the First Commandment (Exodus 20:3), which the author presents here as a universal spiritual necessity rather than just a legalistic rule.</note>

<page-num>202</page-num>

# THE MINISTRY #

Independent of a thousand other instructive lessons that nature is charged by **supreme love** <note>original: "amour suprême"; a term the author uses to refer to the Divine or the Creator's active benevolence</note> to transmit daily and physically to the human soul, we are intimately convinced that each thing, simply to have a name among men, must have made its own revelation. Thus, the religious practices that one sees universally in use among men do not allow us to doubt that this supreme love has also opened, in this regard, some kind of path of **rehabilitation** <term>rehabilitation: the process of restoring the human soul to its original, pre-fallen state of spiritual power and clarity</term> for the human soul, although enormous piles of rubble have so accumulated over these restorative sources that they can barely be recognized.

And even when we feel this rigorous principle—that it is necessary for a thing to make its own revelation, without which we could never have known it, nor repeated it, nor transmitted it to ourselves—we will see that there is nothing, even down to **politics** and all the **civil institutions** of men, for which we would not find the model outside of us and above us. Yes, if there were not legions, different degrees of superiority, leaders, and governments on high, we would have none of those institutions among us. And even man here below walks under the eye and the aegis of **invisible powers** from whom he receives everything, but whom he hardly seeks to know, and in whom he is no longer disposed to believe, by virtue of becoming intoxicated with his own power; but if he thus becomes intoxicated with his own power, it is because, in fact, he was meant to have a more real one; it is because he was meant to have an **empire** and faithful, submissive subjects.

A positive and known law that I recall here for the friends of wisdom, as one of the most useful torches shining in their path, is that despite the innumerable diversity of so many beings and so many classes composing the universe, there are specific **unities of action** <note>original: "unités d'action." In Saint-Martin's philosophy, these are spiritual or natural forces that act uniformly upon a specific category or "class" of beings.</note> which encompass entire classes and operate on the individuals within those classes by virtue of their **natural analogy** <note>original: "analogie naturelle." This refers to the inherent correspondence or likeness between things that subjects them to the same laws.</note>.

This is why in all the productions of nature, there are genera, species, and families where everything bears the imprint of this unity of action, according to its class.

The powers and faculties of our **spirit** <term>Spirit (Esprit): Here referring to the human intellect and its higher cognitive/spiritual functions.</term> would undoubtedly exhibit the same law, showing a sort of uniformity in the movements of human thought, which reduces all its systems to a limited number of **theorems** and **axioms**, and all its institutions to fundamental formulas that hardly vary. The medicinal art, morality, politics, deliberative and scientific assemblies, and finally everything pertaining to the religious order, and—if I dare say so—the infernal order itself, would all come in crowds to testify in favor of this principle.

By this law, the same physical action that governs the blood of man also governs the blood of animals, because the body of man belongs to their class. This, it seems to me, is where one can derive, in general, an insight concerning the spirit behind the institution of sacrifices.

This same perspective can guide us in discovering the specific spirit which was intended to direct the various types of **sacrifices of the Hebrews** in detail, such as the sacrifices for sin and atonement, the sacrifices called **peace offerings**, and even those whose goal was a holy reconciliation with God, and the union of man with Him, confirmed by the perceptible signs of their covenant.

The simple **law of transposition** <term>law of transposition: the spiritual principle of moving a "stain" or influence from one vessel (man) to another (the sacrifice) to neutralize it</term> of which we have just spoken, suffices to make us conceive what the spirit of the sin offering was: casting impurities into the region of disorder and onto the enemy who had caused them.

The **peace offering** would seem to have the goal of giving strength to man to resist this enemy, and even to prevent his attacks.

Now, if it was from him that these various actions expected a wise administration to maintain them in their primitive order and office—that is to say, that he should develop and manifest in them the divine wonders of which they were the depositories, and which were to serve the sacrifices of glory—it must be that by having gone astray himself, his fall was able to drag all these various actions or powers into a state of subjection and violence for which they were not made, and which is for them like a kind of death.

For in the example just cited, it is always man who must be the object of our focus; we need only observe that the dual types <note>original: "doubles types," referring to symbolic archetypes or prophetic figures.</note> concerning him are divided between two different nations: the Egyptians and the Hebrews. One depicts man in his fall and his state of condemnation, while the other depicts him within his law of deliverance and his return toward that sublime station from which he descended.

However, we do not employ the laws and ceremonies of the Hebrews as the base and foundation of the theory we are presenting. This theory rests, first and foremost, upon the nature of both ancient and present man—that is to say, upon our grandeur and our misery. When the theory subsequently finds testimonies on earth that support and sustain it, it makes use of them not as proof, but as confirmation.

Accordingly, we have no need to resort to the Holy Scriptures to discover how far back the origin of sacrifices reaches. For *sacrifices of glory*, the origin traces back to the era prior to the transgression <note>original: "prévarication," a term often used in mystical literature to describe the initial spiritual "breach of trust" or Fall of man.</note> of man; for *bloody and expiatory sacrifices*, it traces back to the moment when guilty man began to see the path of his deliverance crack open before him. This moment is the very same in which he was permitted to come and inhabit the earth; for previously, buried like a child in an abyss <note>original: "abyme," a recurring term in this work for the state of spiritual darkness or the material container of the fallen soul.</note>, he could not have at his disposal the materials for sacrifices, as he did not even have the use of his own faculties.

His primary destiny was to be linked to all of nature throughout the entire duration of the work he would have had to fulfill, had he maintained his station.

Despite his fall, man always found himself bound to this same nature <note>In the author’s theosophical context, "nature" refers to the material and elemental realm that became a prison or a "weight" after the Fall.</note> which he could not escape, and whose painful weight was further increased by the dominion that man had allowed his enemy <note>A reference to the Adversary or the power of evil.</note> to take over nature and over himself. In the time of his deliverance, he was given the permission and the power to employ them for his advancement; a point we cannot doubt, based on all the preceding observations.

But here there is a difference: it is that while our ideas are variable, the words we use to express them can vary as well; whereas the properties of beings being fixed, the numbers or the figures that indicate them cannot be subject to changes.

However, mathematics, although far from knowing and employing these <term>fixed numbers: inherent numerical values that represent the essential qualities or "signatures" of a being, as opposed to abstract mathematical units</term>, offer us a glimpse of them in the free or arbitrary numbers they use; for they constantly apply, it is true, these free and arbitrary numbers to the values of objects they submit to their speculations; and once they have attached them to these values, the numbers are merely their signs and representatives, and if they were detached from them, they would be nothing more. But it is we who have invented <term>pure mathematics: the study of numbers and shapes as mental abstractions, independent of any physical application</term>, or abstraction made of all application.

Nature does not know this kind of mathematics. Nature is the continual union of geometrical laws with fixed numbers that we do not know. Man, in his thought, can consider these laws independently of their fixed numbers; but nature is the effective execution of these laws, and it is foreign to all abstraction. <note>The author suggests that while humans can think of the number "4" in isolation, in the natural world, a "4" never exists without being attached to a specific quality or substance.</note>

Finally, the third class of these abominations is that of superstitions and idolatries of all kinds. The forms of every species that irregular action <note>Saint-Martin uses the term "irregular action" to describe spiritual influences or manifestations that operate outside of the divine order, often leading to deception or theurgy.</note> knew how to assume in order to corrupt sacrifices and lead man astray, were the primary sources of material idolatry. This occurred because the practitioners <note>original: "opérans"; those performing ritual or theurgic acts to contact the spiritual realm.</note> who received these manifestations were led, by a natural inclination, to honor those living animals and all other natural substances that had connections with the forms under which the irregular action had shown itself; and it is from this that the worship of so many peoples for different beings and for different objects of their cult originated.

From there to figurative idolatry, or that of images, there is but a step; since a thousand circumstances often forced the substitution of the image of the idol for the idol itself, the veneration of the people passed very easily from the idol to the image and the statue.

The origin of apotheoses <note>original: "apothéoses"; the elevation of a human being to the rank of a god.</note> is likewise found in this source, because the practitioner was often mistaken for the very being who was the object of the worship. Thus, among almost all peoples, one recognizes a visible Divinity and an invisible Divinity; in the North, one finds two Odins: one, the supreme God; the other, a conqueror; similarly, one finds two Jupiters among the Greeks, two Zoroasters among the Persians, two Zamolxis among the Thracians, etc. (*Edda. 1787, p. 59.*) <note>The *Edda* is a collection of Old Norse poems and texts; Saint-Martin is citing a specific 18th-century edition to support his theory of "doubled" historical and divine figures.</note>

The blood and the voice of the prophets had led the Hebrew people only to the approaches to the temple and the divine region, because the time had not yet come when man could enter the temple itself. Thus, there were a great number of prophets employed in this preparatory work, and the hand that led them traced different paths for them in those wildernesses they were frequenting for the first time. This is why, each walking on their own particular path, they did not always know the final goal toward which their prophecies tended, which was unveiled to them only in fragments and as if from a distance.

Likewise, the people—who had not recognized the **law of the spirit** within the <term>Levitical ceremonies<note>The complex system of rituals and sacrifices performed by the priests of the tribe of Levi, as described in the Old Testament.</note></term>, even though it was contained therein—also failed to recognize the **divine law** that was announced to them in the law of the spirit or in the prophecies. Continuing to walk in darkness, they thus arrived at the era of universal deliverance, of which not only had the prophets never ceased to speak (each according to what they were permitted to know), but which was also indicated in the <term>books of Moses<note>The Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible.</note></term>, particularly in the **blessings of Jacob**; for if the people had truly made a careful study of these books, they should have reflected seriously when they saw the temporal power of Judah pass into the hands of the <term>Idumean<note>A person from Idumea (Edom); here referring to Herod the Great, whose rise to power as a non-Judean was seen by many as the fulfillment of the prophecy that the "scepter" would depart from Judah when the Messiah was to appear.</note></term> named **Herod**.

<margin>S</margin>
Now, who could have taught him this profound and salutary truth? It was not the sacrifices of animals, since these animals, devoid of morality, gave him no idea of a voluntary immolation; and bringing only their physical bodies to the altar of <term>burnt offerings<note>original: "holocaustes" — the ancient Jewish ritual sacrifices described in the Old Testament.</note></term>, they could only untie man from his external and physical chains, just as they themselves were.

<margin>1</margin>
Nor was it the sacrifices and death of the prophets, because they did not go voluntarily to their execution, even though they may have gone with resignation; because this execution, for those who underwent it, was only an uncertain consequence of their mission, and was not the mission itself; because they were sent only to announce the dawn of the eternal day of man's deliverance, and not to restore him fully to liberty; because, finally, they themselves desired to penetrate into this great day that they announced without knowing it, and which they only glimpsed through scattered rays, and as if by flashes of the spirit.

# ON THE MAN-SPIRIT

Let us remember that we were dead, and that it was necessary for the repairer <term>the repairer: Saint-Martin’s characteristic title for Christ, emphasizing his role in "repairing" the broken relationship between humanity and the Divine.</term> to enter into our death to make himself similar to us; but just as in entering our death, he did not cease to be life; so in making himself similar to us, he did not cease to be our unique principle; thus he could not die without rising again, and without raising us up with him, in order to make us similar to him; this resurrection was necessary so that we could taste life, praise life, and celebrate it, which was and will eternally be the goal of the existence of every spiritual being formed in the image of the sovereign author of all beings.

The institution of the Last Supper <note>original: "la cène." While referring to the Eucharist or Holy Communion, Saint-Martin interprets this sacrament as an internal, spiritual transformation rather than just an outward ritual.</note> thus had the objective of retracing in us this death and this resurrection even before the dissolution of our corporeal essences—that is to say, to teach us at once to die with the repairer and to rise again with him. Thus this religious ceremony, considered in its sublimity, can become in us, in reality, a production, an emanation, a creation, a regeneration, or a universal and perpetual resurrection; and it can, I say, transform us into the kingdom of God, and ensure that we are no more than one with God.

However, it would be very essential for the celebrant <note>original: "l'opérant." In Saint-Martin's context, this refers to the person performing the spiritual "operation" or rite, suggesting an active, theurgical participation.</note> to repeat unceasingly to the faithful these words of the teacher: *the flesh and the blood are of no use; my words are spirit and life* <note>A reference to John 6:63: "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life."</note>; for how many spirits has the letter of other words killed! It is necessary that in the celebrant, as in us, the idea and the word of flesh and blood be abolished—that is to say, we must ascend, like the repairer, to the region of the pure element which was our primitive body, and which ultimately contains the eternal <term>SOPHIA</term> <term>SOPHIA: From the Greek for "Wisdom." In Christian theosophy, Sophia represents the divine mirror or the celestial bride; for Saint-Martin, she is the spiritual substance that humanity lost during the Fall and must regain.</term>.

# OF THE SPIRIT-MAN.

...all those anthropomorphic <note>original: "antromorphiques." Relating to the attribution of human characteristics to divine or natural entities.</note> representations which fill the world.

If artists represent all the virtues, both celestial and terrestrial, to us under human forms, whether masculine or feminine; if poets personify all the gods and goddesses of the Empyrean <note>The Empyrean refers to the highest heaven, the residence of the Divine and the source of pure light and fire.</note>, and all the powers of nature and the elements; finally, if the followers of various religions and the idolaters fill their temples with human statues, the principle behind all these customs is not illusory or abusive, as are the results that have stemmed from them.

The primitive human form <note>In Saint-Martin's theosophy, the "primitive human form" is the spiritual, glorious body man possessed before his "fall" into matter—an archetype for the entire universe.</note> should indeed show itself and dominate in all regions. Man being the image and the extract of the generating center of all that exists, his form was the seat where all the powers of all the regions came to exercise and manifest their action; in a word, the point where all the properties and all the *virtues* <term>virtues: In this context, "virtues" (vertus) refers to active spiritual powers or innate properties, rather than just moral qualities.</term> of things corresponded.

<margin>B</margin>

Thus, all the representations of himself that he creates through his own industry do nothing more than trace for him pictures of what he could and should be, and figuratively replace him within the measures <note>This refers to the spiritual proportions or "stature" man held in his original state.</note> where he no longer exists in reality.

For, let us say in passing, when scholars compare the body of man with the bodies of beasts, and call this comparative anatomy, our true body has nothing to do with this comparative anatomy, which, indeed, teaches us nothing else except that we resemble other animals.

It would be, on the contrary, our superior and non-animal body that would need to be compared with our animal body, if one wished to have the true knowledge of ourselves.

It is to this important occupation that what we might call the first age of the law of the spirit is consecrated; and this obligation is so rigorous for us that if we fail in it, we soon fall back into various forms of servitude analogous to our transgressions; but also, when overwhelmed by the yoke of our tyrants, we call upon the supreme hand, and it raises up various liberators who restore us to our paths.

This is a representative image of what we must do in our first age of the law of the spirit, where we must separate ourselves from everything that would prevent us from growing and acquiring the gifts necessary so that one day the *nations* may be blessed in us.

Thus, it is the void of his spirit that causes him to fall into discouragement, by making him believe that lost time can never be repaired. This may be true for things that are done only in time and by time; but is it the same for things that are done by the spirit and for the spirit? If the spirit has no time and knows no time, can a single act performed by the spirit and for the spirit not restore to the soul everything it might have neglected to gather, or even everything it might have lost through its negligence?

It is here, above all, that we must remember the eleventh hour <note>A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16), where those who begin work at the very end of the day receive the same reward as those who started early, symbolizing divine mercy and the timeless nature of spiritual effort.</note>; but we must also see that if he who was called then received even more than his wages, it is because he had at least worked during that eleventh hour, without which he would have received nothing at all,
