...and thus we would have no claim to the reward, if we did not fill this eleventh hour—which remains to us after having spent the other hours in vain—by laboring at the work of the spirit <note>original: "l'œuvre de l'esprit." In Saint-Martin's theosophical system, this refers to the "Great Work" of spiritual reintegration, where man actively works to restore his lost divine image.</note>.

Since the Fall <note>original: "la chûte." The primordial event in which humanity descended from a state of spiritual splendor into the constraints of the material world.</note>, we can all only be laborers of the eleventh hour, which began, in effect, at the very moment we were stripped of our rights. The *ten hours* that precede this epoch have remained far behind us and are, as it were, lost to us, so that our entire earthly life is really for us only the eleventh hour of our eternal and true day, which encompasses the universal circle of things. Let us judge from this whether we have a single moment to lose.

But likewise, everything necessary for us to discharge the labor of this eleventh hour usefully and profitably is provided to us in abundance; plans, materials, instruments—nothing is refused to us. Even the obstacles and the dangers we encounter in our labor, which become crosses for us when we shrink from them, become rungs and means of ascension when we overcome them; for Wisdom <note>original: "la sagesse." Often personified in this tradition as Divine Sophia, the guiding intelligence of the universe.</note>, which exposes us to them, has no intention other than to make us triumph.

Yes, if we faithfully kept our post, the enemy would never enter the place, however powerful he might be. But we must also guard all its passages with such sustained activity that, wherever he presents himself, he finds us vigilant and strong enough to resist him. A single moment of negligence on our part is enough for the enemy—who never sleeps—to make a breach, mount the assault, and seize the citadel <note>original: "la citadelle." A common mystical metaphor for the human soul or the inner spiritual "center" that must be defended against dark influences.</note>.

Let us therefore take heart. If our spiritual rehabilitation <note>original: "réhabilitation spirituelle." In the context of Martinism, this refers to the process of "reintegration," or returning to the divine state from which humanity fell.</note> truly demands all our care, we can also regard it as assured, provided we determine to undertake it; for the illness of the human soul—if I may permit myself to express it thus—is but a kind of **stopped perspiration**; and supreme wisdom never ceases to pass into us salutary and powerful **sudorifics** <term>sudorifics: medicines that induce sweating. Saint-Martin uses this medical metaphor to describe spiritual purifications that help "flush out" the impurities of the material world.</term> which tend constantly to restore circulation and order in our fluids <note>original: "nos liqueurs." This refers to the "humors" or vital fluids believed in 18th-century physiology to govern health; here, it is a metaphor for the soul's internal harmony.</note>.

Even death, which is also part of our work, is directed and graduated with the same wisdom that governs all divine operations. Our material bonds break progressively, and in an almost imperceptible manner. Infants, being still entirely under the weight of their matter, have no idea of death, because indeed matter does not know what death is, just as it also does not know what life or spirit is.

Young people, in whom this spirit or life begins to pierce through their matter, are more or less frightened by death, depending on whether they are more or less imbued with this spirit, or life, and according to how much the contrast between their spirit and their matter is felt within them.

Mature men and the elderly, in whom their spirit or life has reached its full development, and who have faithfully followed the law of their being, find themselves so filled with the fruits of their work when the end of their career arrives, that they see—not only without fear and without regret, but even with joy—the demolition of their **material envelope**.

limit and his nothingness. <note>This follows from the previous page, completing a thought about how the "inferior spirit" chains the soul to its own limitations and void.</note> From this, three instructions may be deduced.

The first is that the <term>inferior spirit: In Saint-Martin's philosophy, these are lower spiritual forces or astral influences that appeal to man's fallen nature and sensory desires rather than his divine origin.</term> deceives us twice over: first, by showing us spiritually those delights that we can no longer truly know in our nature except through matter; and second, in that this matter leaves us far short of those delights shown to us spiritually. Now, only a disordered spirit could contribute to such disharmonies and disproportions. A well-ordered spirit would show us—though always through images—what portion of delights ought to belong to our spirit in our earthly relationships, and what the illusion is of those delights that belong only to our matter. By this means, our two beings <note>The "two beings" refers to the spiritual man and the physical/material man.</note> would not be deceived, because order would reign in both.

The second instruction is that which teaches us why men here who are advanced in age, but who have made themselves the playthings of their senses, still enjoy in their depraved spirits all the delights that their matter can no longer experience; for this is but a prolongation of their first affection, or of this action of the inferior spirit.

Finally, the third instruction is that which teaches us the source of the disgusts that follow our illusions; for it was not through matter that we were meant to enjoy.

Does man wish to consider himself in relation to knowledge, or in relation to his spirit? He will encounter new subjects for lamentation; for he will see himself surrendered to systematic and <note>Saint-Martin uses "systematic knowledge" (connoissances systématiques) to describe purely academic or intellectual sciences that ignore the spiritual heart of reality.</note>

### *Of the Word.*

If there were not a harmonized power that eternally generated itself, we would never see order reborn and succeed the alterations of all that constitutes the circle of things, as happens before our eyes at every moment. So, let us say it loudly: there is an <term>eternal Word</term> <note>original: "éternelle parole." ### OF THE MAN-SPIRIT

It is through the <term>Word</term> <note>original: "la parole." In Saint-Martin’s philosophy, the Word is the creative, governing expression of Divine Will, similar to the Logos.</note> that God governs the course of his general spiritual and temporal alliance: it is only when this alliance has acquired the necessary sum of forces through the attraction of its powerful divine elements, that the Word allows it to trigger its explosion, and that the Word carries itself into the torrent of this explosion, the better to make its salutary substances penetrate into the regions that await them. This is one of the wonders of <term>active numbers</term> <note>original: "nombres actifs." For Saint-Martin, numbers were not mere quantities but spiritual qualities or laws that represent the hidden workings of the Divine Word in the universe.</note> which, however, are nothing in themselves, as we have seen previously, but which faithfully represent the hidden path of the Word and its immeasurable properties.

It is through the Word that God also forms a particular and continual alliance within the realm of vegetation and terrestrial nature, where all productions are preceded by every gradation of activity, of germination, and of growth. These stages attract one another reciprocally and culminate in an <term>explosion</term> <note>Saint-Martin uses "explosion" to describe a sudden, vital manifestation of life or spirit—the moment a potentiality becomes a reality.</note>, whether as a flowering or a birth, occurring when the eye or the center of life in each thing has dissipated the obstacles surrounding it and can finally enter into its rightful state.

Just as all these bases of action are scattered throughout nature, so too are all the seeds of the sciences scattered throughout all of humanity: we lack only an analogous language, or the Word, to communicate them to us. If we were careful to diligently cultivate these seeds, they would themselves produce the language that would serve to transmit their fruits to us; but our impatience carries us away, and instead of waiting for the fructification...

# OF THE MAN-SPIRIT. <note>original: "De l'Homme-Esprit." The "Man-Spirit" is Saint-Martin's term for the human being restored to their original divine vocation and power.</note>

What joy for you, when you succeed in engendering, in the world of truth and light, a man who resembles you, and who is your cherished son!

The true word is universally in anguish <note>original: "angoisse." In the mystical tradition of Jacob Boehme, which Saint-Martin followed, "anguish" refers to the productive tension or "birth pangs" necessary for spiritual manifestation or transformation.</note>; thus, we can receive or operate nothing except through anguish; likewise, everything that exists in the visible realm does not cease to physically demonstrate the word in anguish; thus, we should not flee internal anguish; for it is only the words of anguish that are profitable, that sow and that engender, because they alone are the expression of life and love.

Man, do not fear to see an announcement of this rigorous law in the cries of your mother when she brings you into the light of day, as well as in the tears you shed from the moment of your birth. Learn from this also what it must have cost the source of refreshment <note>original: "rafraîchissement." A technical term in Saint-Martin’s theosophy referring to the divine grace or "cooling" influence that tempers the harsh fire of the material or fallen state.</note> to procreate itself within the form of your spiritual alteration <note>original: "altération spirituelle." This refers to the corrupted state of human nature following the Fall.</note>, and to make itself of your kind. But compare your active and free temporal life to the one you led in your mother's womb, and see if it does not even provide you with enjoyments and an existence that make you forget your first tears; and learn by this what you should expect from the slightest impressions that the true anguish can make you feel.

Dispose also your eyes and your intelligence to see, admire, and understand what stems every day from the particular anguish of refreshment or of the word, and what will stem in the future from their general anguish; for the results of all these anguishes are as certain as they are immeasurable.

Such is generally our situation here below; we are all under a curative and medicinal regime, whether by the effect of the great alteration <note>original: "grande altération." In Saint-Martin's philosophy, this refers to the Fall of Man and the subsequent corruption of the human state and the natural world.</note>, or as a consequence of our own transgressions: when we observe all that is commanded for our **spiritual health**, we are, in doing so, only useful to ourselves. Saint-Martin makes a grammatical and philosophical distinction: "serving God" (personal devotion) is for the benefit of the individual, whereas "serving *to* God" (being of use to God) means becoming an active tool for the divine purpose.</note>

It is when we are **regenerated**, and when we can fulfill the various **ministries** of our master, that we are considered truly to serve God; for it is then that we can, by means of our own sorrows, feel and know by experience what the **sufferings of the Word** <note>original: "douleurs de la parole." Let us therefore close within us the doors of evil and of nothingness, so that the living regions may come to penetrate us.

When the **hand of God** is upon man, and when it is for his punishment, man is bound in all his faculties. He is tormented by restlessness and the need for action and movement, and by the unbearable ***Gehenna*** <term>Gehenna: Historically a name for hell; here, Saint-Martin uses it to describe a state of intense internal spiritual pressure or "violent contraction" felt by the soul.</term> which holds his entire being in a violent contraction; but he remains in inactivity, and everything is suspended for him.

When it is for the progress of the work, and for the advancement of the word, the weight of the hand of God torments him as well, but it is through the impatience for justice; and the ***Gehenna*** he experiences makes him advance each day into the living and luminous regions of **spiritual activity**.

<summary>Saint-Martin distinguishes between spiritual self-care and true divine service, arguing that we only truly serve God when we are regenerated enough to share in the "sufferings of the Word." ...all fluctuations and all illusions <note>original: "prestiges." In the 18th century, this term often referred to deceptive appearances or magical delusions rather than modern "prestige" or status.</note>; but ensure that your words are for him both a torch that guides him, and an anchor that steadies and reassures him against the storms.

What, then, are the essential laws of the administration of the word <note>Saint-Martin uses "the word" (la parole) to mean more than just speech; it is the expression of the soul’s creative power, modeled after the divine Logos.</note> toward your fellow man?

It is to respect human intelligence enough to feel that it should only associate with intelligence, and that one should present nothing to it that is not worthy of it, and that cannot increase its riches.

It is to persuade yourself that this human intelligence must be treated like the great personages of the Orient, whom one never approaches without having gifts to offer them. <note>This metaphor reflects the 18th-century European fascination with Eastern courtly traditions, suggesting that every conversation should be treated as a formal, respectful exchange of spiritual value.</note>

It is to ensure that you always add to the light and the virtues of those who converse with you, and that your word always offers benefits to those who hear it.

It is to speak to them only of solid objects and profound truths, instead of feeding them only on frivolous tales and narrations, since these frivolous tales and narrations are composed of time—where there is only the past and the future—whereas great truths are always present, like axioms; thus, they do not belong to time, but to the permanent and eternal realm.

It is to distribute your word with sobriety, because it is only bad causes that require so many words to defend them.

It is to never forget that the word is the light of the infinite, which must never do anything but increase.

### OF THE SPIRIT-MAN

...generally [derived] from the habits, the locales, the customs<note>original: "mœurs" — a term encompassing the social habits, morals, and behavioral norms of a society.</note>, and the affections of the peoples among whom you live.

This is why you find it just as easy to depict falsehood as truth.

If from style we move to the heart of things, we see that writers, critics, and even moralists seem only occupied with painting for us the vices and defects of humanity; one would say their only task were to fill us with hatred for our species, or at least to give us nothing but contempt and disdain for it, by showing us only its blameworthy and repulsive sides. They do not reflect on how much, in doing so, they harm both themselves and us.

First, their pride is the only thing that gains from this work, because it is hardly possible to know the faults of others so well without secretly glorifying oneself, and proving in some way, through such remarks, that one is exempt from those very faults.

Second, they are unaware of how much more they would do for their glory and for our happiness if they instead painted the beautiful colors of the human species, which can always be recognized even in the midst of the mire where it is buried. It is true that God sometimes lends us our own thought; that is to say, He leaves us to ourselves, just as a master allows a few moments of recreation and liberty to his servants after they have completed his work. One might even believe that this is the case for the vast majority of this world's thinkers, who indeed appear to be like schoolchildren on holiday. But these schoolchildren, or these servants, are on holiday and at recreation without having previously performed their classroom duty, nor the master’s task; they consume their moments of liberty in places of dispute, quarreling and fighting amongst themselves, often even disparaging the teacher<note>original: "régent." Writers filled with talent have tried to depict for us the glorious effects of Christianity. But although I read their works with frequent admiration, nevertheless, finding nothing in them of what their subject would, it seems to me, oblige them to give us—seeing that they sometimes replace principles with eloquence, or even, if you will, with poetry—I read them, at times, only with caution. Nonetheless, if I make a few remarks on their writings, it is certainly neither as an atheist nor as an unbeliever that I dare to allow myself to do so. I have long fought the same enemies that these authors attack with courage; and my principles in this regard have, with age, only acquired more consistency.

When people credit Christianity with the progress of the arts, and particularly with the refinement of literature and poetry, they attribute to it a merit that this Christianity is very far from claiming. It was not to teach men how to write poems, or to distinguish themselves through charming literary productions, that the Word <note>Saint-Martin uses "la parole" (the Word) here to refer to the divine Logos or the creative principle of God.</note> came into the world: it came, not to make the human spirit shine in the eyes of its peers, but to make the eternal and universal spirit shine in the eyes of all the vast infinities.

Why does Christianity have no need to concern itself with all these talents of men? It is because it dwells among divine wonders, and to sing of them, it has no need to seek how it shall express itself; these wonders provide it with the affections, the idea, and the expression all at once. Thus, it alone can answer the observation made by eloquent writers: *One does not know where the human spirit went to seek such things; all the paths to reach this sublime <note>The "sublime" was a major concept in 18th-century aesthetics, referring to a greatness beyond all possibility of calculation, measurement, or imitation.</note> are unknown.* For in that order of things, the human spirit sought nothing, since the spirit of Christianity gave it everything.

But what is more, Catholicism—to which the name of Christianity is too easily given—this Catholicism, I say, is not itself what produced the development of literature and the arts. It was not in Catholicism, nor through it, that modern poets and artists were formed: they looked to the masterpieces of antiquity, which was pagan, and they sought to imitate them; but as they lived in the midst of the institutions of Catholicism, it is not surprising

God grant that he had never emerged from this dust, for he should have no other dwelling, and he should have constantly left the field open to the Word <note>original: "la parole." In Saint-Martin's philosophy, the "Word" or "Speech" is the divine creative power that humans originally possessed and must work to recover.</note>.

Let us see, indeed, what art has produced by approaching great truths.

The eloquent writer in question <note>Referring to Chateaubriand.</note> may go into raptures over the awakening of Adam, and say that Milton would never have reached such heights had he not known the true religion: I would respond that if Milton had known true Christianity, which is the Word, he would have portrayed Adam in different colors.

Art has no other secrets than to make comparisons based on the objects made known to it. This art teaches us that a child is a being who *awakens to life, whose eyes open, and who knows not from where he came.* It is upon this example that Milton traced the portrait of Adam: he makes of him nothing more than a grown child, except that he gives him a sublime sense of his nature and eminent powers of naming things, which are denied to the child; and one would be at a loss to say why, if the father possessed them, the child would not have them also, since the fruit must take after the tree that generated it.

Now, it is also from the "child-man" and the "savage-man" that the materialists and the ideologues <note>The "Idéologues" were a group of French Enlightenment thinkers (such as Destutt de Tracy) who believed all human ideas originated solely from physical sensations.</note> have drawn the fragile systems of their sensations, of the origin of languages, etc.; and it is by stopping there that they have finally animalized our entire being. But the Bible (for I can say only that here), which is supposed to have served as Milton's guide, shows us Adam in a different light.

Saint-Martin argues that Chateaubriand’s literary praise of Milton’s Adam fails to recognize the true spiritual nature of the first man, treating him instead like a "large child" rather than a being of "the Word."</meta>

# OF THE SPIRIT-MAN

->God [grant] that he had never emerged from this dust, for he should have no other dwelling, and he ought to have constantly left the field free for the Word. <note>original: "la parole." For Saint-Martin, "the Word" is not just speech, but the creative, divine faculty that humans lost at the Fall and must recover.</note><-

Let us see, in fact, what art has produced when approaching great truths.

The eloquent writer in question <note>Refers to Chateaubriand.</note> may well go into ecstasies regarding the awakening of Adam, and say that Milton would not have reached these heights had he not known the true religion; I shall reply that if Milton had known true Christianity, which is the Word, he would have painted Adam in different colors.

Art has no other secrets than to make comparisons based on objects surrendered to its knowledge. This art teaches us that the child is a being who *awakens to life, whose eyes open, and who does not know from whence he came.* It is upon this example that Milton traced the portrait of Adam: he makes him nothing but a large child, except that he gives him a sublime sense of his nature and eminent powers to name things, which is denied to the child; and one would be embarrassed to say why, the father having possessed them, the child would not have them as well, since the fruit must take after its generative tree.

Now, it is also from the child-man and the savage-man that the materialists and the ideologues <note>The "Ideologues" (Idéologues) were a group of French Enlightenment philosophers who argued that all ideas derive from physical sensations; Saint-Martin strongly opposed this reductionist view of the human soul.</note> have drawn the fragile systems of their sensations, of the origin of languages, etc.; and it is by stopping there that they have finally animalized our entire being. But the Bible (for I can say no more than that here), which is supposed to have served as Milton's guide, shows us Adam in another light.

<summary>Saint-Martin criticizes John Milton's portrayal of Adam in "Paradise Lost," arguing that treating the first man as a naive "child" ignores his original divine stature. He further links this literary failing to the errors of materialist philosophers who reduce human consciousness to mere physical sensation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Saint-Martin’s analysis of the biblical account of creation, specifically focusing on the state of Adam before the "deep sleep" mentioned in Genesis. # THE MINISTRY

First, one may believe that Adam, upon emerging from the hands of the Creator, was not at all subject to sleep; for it was only after he had given names to every thing that the Creator sent a sleep upon him, during which the woman was extracted from his bones or from his powerful essences.

Secondly, it is probable that this sleep and this extraction were the consequence of some alteration already begun within Adam, since the Creator had said, following the creation (at the end of the first chapter of Genesis), that all the works He had made were *good*; yet He says (in the second chapter) that *it is not good that man should be alone.*

Thirdly, whether this precise application of names to things was performed by Adam upon emerging from the hands of the Creator, or only after this alteration had begun (a choice which the text, combined with the preceding reflection, seems to allow, although [spiritual] principles exclude the second hypothesis), it is certain, according to the letter <note>The "letter" refers to the literal text of the Bible.</note>, that this application of names to things took place before the sleep.

In that case, Adam must have then enjoyed a great light and a vast and effective knowledge <note>original: "science." In Saint-Martin's context, this refers to an intuitive, divine understanding of the inner nature of things, rather than modern empirical science.</note>, since the Creator had established him over all the works of His hands, had installed him Himself in the garden of delights <note>A traditional term for the Garden of Eden.</note>, and had charged him to cultivate it, delivering to him all the plants with which it was filled, and even the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from which He forbade him to eat.

Thus, Adam did not need to awaken to life; on the contrary, it was he who awakened life

Now, how would they have known pure love if they were already under the animal law? Doubtless they did not then have that *shameless* modesty which is only a secondary modesty of education; but they had a profound shame, based on the comparison of the bestial state in which they found themselves with the state they had just lost; for it was then that their eyes were opened to their debasing degradation, and closed to divine wonders.

In general, I find that when writers and poets have seized upon the riches of Holy Scripture, they have corrupted rather than embellished them, either by mixing them with false colors, or by weakening them through long-windedness, because they were not guided in their undertaking by the true spirit of Christianity; thus, they have never shone more than when they were content to show these riches in their simplicity and literal integrity. It is because, in this work, Racine did nothing more, so to speak, than copy Scripture.

# THE MINISTRY

For however much the learned critics of literature may praise the art with which a poet has ordered his work, the common people <note>original: "le vulgaire." In Saint-Martin's time, this referred to the general public or those without specialized education, rather than being a derogatory term.</note> are, as it were, strangers to these kinds of secrets. Yet they are not strangers to the simple and sublime beauties contained within the Scriptures; and the more these beauties are presented to them in their nakedness, the more certain one is to strike a chord. Consider the imposing effect produced in the theater by this simple verse, the spirit of which is found on every page of the Bible:

> *I fear God..... and have no other fear?* <note>original: "Je crains Dieu ..... et n'ai point d'autre crainte ?" This is a famous line from Jean Racine’s 1691 play *Athalie* (Act 1, Scene 1), often cited as a pinnacle of French classical religious drama.</note>

But at the same time, if one wishes to judge how little fruit these riches bear for Christianity when in the hands of literary men, one only has to observe how the success of the most beautiful thoughts and maxims—those most suited to the true needs of our being—is reduced to nothing in the theater. The spectator who hears them—but who, like the poet, has only his external man <note>Saint-Martin uses the term "external man" to describe the surface-level self that engages only with the senses and intellect, as opposed to the "inner man" or the spirit.</note> open within him—feels a slight impression, a sort of sentimental emotion that transports him for the moment. However, having no deep roots and resembling little more than a muscular sensation, this feeling ends at the tips of his nerves with a round of applause, and evaporates into thin air. Thus, once the play is over, the spectators go away to plunge back into their usual nothingness and futilities, without even remembering what they felt, and even less profiting from it.

Now, what we see happening in the theater for the spectator is also what happens for the reader of beautiful works of eloquence and poetry that rely on the treasures of the Scriptures and the sanctity of Catholicism. It would be far worse if they spoke of true Christianity, or of the eternal Word and the eternal

And what I say here of men of letters in general unfortunately applies only too well to religious writers as well; this is why their science has become nothing but an art in their hands. For if they seem to join some ideas of another kind to these physical objects that they include in their descriptions, it is commonly to awaken in us the impressions of a secondary sensitivity <term>secondary sensitivity: original: "sensibilité secondaire." There is another descriptive genre that seems to me to have its abuses as well. It is that by which clever literary critics exhaust themselves in dissecting the beautiful passages of great authors; and I cannot help but tell them: If these passages carry their beauties within themselves, I have no need of your help to taste them. I have even less need of your dissections. I would have less pleasure if I knew so much why I have it. You deceive me by cooling my enjoyments, just as the descriptive poets of nature deceive me by daily giving me their personal fictions in place of nature's true intentions.

For Christianity to truly favor what one ought to call descriptive poetry, poets would have to become what Adam was before his sleep <note>In Saint-Martin's thought, Adam's "sleep" represents the beginning of the Fall, where he lost his direct, intuitive command over nature and his ability to see the "life" or essence within all things.</note>; that is to say that, like him, they would know how to awaken life in beings, instead of only entertaining us with what is, in a way, merely the anatomy of these beings, or even their external form.

->A<-

...tually in all our acts, even in the efforts we make to deny it.

But it is not so much these two articles <note>Referring to the existence of God and the immortality of the soul, mentioned on the preceding page.</note> that offend the dissenters, as it is the entire religious edifice that one wishes to build upon these two foundations; thus, proving the first two points does not prove the positive consequences that one wishes to deduce from them.

Indeed, reasoning and logic only prove the existence of God and that of the soul. The purpose of the religious matter <note>original: "la chose religieuse." Saint-Martin often uses this term to describe the active, lived reality of spiritual connection as opposed to mere theory.</note> must be to prove their relationship and to reunite one with the other; this reunion cannot take place without an internal cooperation on our part, and without the voluntary action of our being. Simple belief in the existence of God and the soul requires no such cooperation.

This is why it is easier to cure a materialist <note>Someone who believes only in physical matter.</note> and an atheist than a deist <note>A deist believes in a creator based on reason but rejects supernatural revelation or a personal relationship with God.</note>. In truth, how can one persuade a deist of the natural source of the religious matter, of its utility, and of its necessity, if not by resting the foundation upon the infirm and dark state of **degraded man**? But how can one reach that point after the harm that human philosophy has done to man? How can one find men capable of leading their fellows along this path?

Let us, then, no longer be surprised that the daily attempts made on behalf of the religious matter are so unfruitful. Let us even agree that when it comes to attacking materialism and atheism, the ordinary teachers still possess only very powerless weapons, since they prove God only through the universe, and they prove the soul only through theological books. How, then, would they prove the soul...

It is this very idea that no doubt led me formerly to say in *The Man of Desire*, no. 166 <note>original: *L'Homme de désir*, a key work by Saint-Martin published in 1790 which uses poetic and reaching language to describe the soul's path.</note>, that the sublime was God, and everything that put us in relationship with Him. I have since read in the works of this same professor: *“What is beautiful, what is great, what is strong admits of the ‘more’ or the ‘less’: there is no such thing in the sublime, etc.”*

I recognized there that his idea and mine on the sublime were the same, except for the conviction I hold that what he and I believe regarding the sublime, we can extend to all the other qualities, virtues, etc., that he excludes from this rule; for it is only in God that all these things are positive <note>In this context, "positive" means absolute, non-comparative, and self-existent, rather than relative to something else.</note>; and the Word is the universal and eternal proclaimer of all these positive sublimities.

It would be to say that we actually see God in everything, and that truly we would see nothing in any objects whatsoever, if the principle of all qualities—that is to say, if God—did not operate actively in them, either by Himself or through His powers.

# OF THE SPIRIT-MAN <note>The full title of the work is *The Ministry of the Spirit-Man* (1802). In Saint-Martin's philosophy, "Ministry" refers to the active, restorative work that a spiritually awakened human performs as an intermediary between God and the world.</note>

This single thing is the desire of God; all other things that lead man astray, man does not truly crave; he is instead their slave or their plaything. On the other hand, the magnificence of his ministry is to be unable to truly and radically act except according to the positive order pronounced to him at every moment, like a master to his servant, and this by the only authority that is equitable, good, consistent, effective, and in conformity with the eternal desire. All the other orders he receives daily, he does not receive as a servant; it is he who provokes them out of self-interest, and often even out of pride, by making himself sovereign. Thus, almost everywhere in this world, servants put themselves in the place of masters.

I can no longer hide here that the divine desire which is felt in the human soul aims to establish an equilibrium between God and the soul, since a desire comes from a separation of analogous substances that need to be united; now, this equilibrium is not a dead and inert effect, but an active development of the divine properties that constitute the human soul, insofar as it is a **universal divine extract**. <note>Saint-Martin views the soul not as a separate, detached creation, but as a "spark" or "extract" containing the qualities of the divine nature itself.</note>

**Destination** seems only ever to be taken in a positive sense; **predestination** has two sides. God often gives *destinations* to men, and it is through this that He has had **elect** <term>Elect: (original: *élus*) Those chosen or set apart by God for a specific spiritual task or ministry.</term> of every kind; but He gives them no *predestination*, because, even in its most favorable light, this word carries with it a sort of constraint that seems to harm **liberty**; and, in its disastrous light, it carries a sort of **fatalism** which would seem to harm **justice**.

It is through misuse that this word was introduced. God may have said to many: *I chose you from your mother's womb, and before the world was;* <note>original: *Je vous ai choisis dès le sein de votre mère , et avant que le monde fût*; a paraphrase of Jeremiah 1:5 and Ephesians 1:4.</note> but it is the spirit of man that has covered this *election* with the word *predestination*; the weak have further altered its meaning, and ignorant fanatics have abused it.

# OF THE SPIRIT-MAN

...to manifest the divine being, yet he has done nothing of the sort. Since his **fall** <note>original: *chûte*; referring to the "Fall of Man" in Eden, which Saint-Martin views as a loss of man's original spiritual power and "primitive line."</note>, whenever he is called to the work, he is merely returning to his natural destination; and if, in those cases, he finds himself superior to his peers by comparison, he is nevertheless only returning to the primitive path in which he should have always walked. Consequently, he does not deserve the name of "predestined" in the sense accepted by the common people; for he is even still far below what he would have been had he remained in his glory, and far below what he will be at the end of time if he arrives there **regenerated** <term>Regenerated: (original: *régénéré*) In Martinist thought, this is the process of restoring the soul to its original divine state through spiritual work and grace.</term>.

Instead of this discouraging system of predestination, could you not have taught us that, on the contrary, it is man who, through his **love**, can even in some way govern God?

<margin><image-desc>A small horizontal squiggle or bracket in the margin.</image-desc></margin>

For those who rush do not see that not only does God conduct Himself according to our needs, but even according to our desires. He is not only with us like a skillful physician, who follows step-by-step the course of an illness and directs his remedies accordingly at every moment, but also like an attentive and tender mother who studies all our tastes, and who, when we strive to please her, holds nothing too dear for us, and sees in us only the cherished object of all her kindness. What mother is not possessed entirely by her son, and does not yield to him when he behaves toward her as he should?

Let us not then be surprised that, far from God being unjust and harsh with us if we were wise, He would, on the contrary, be occupied only with anticipating our every need; and that our love would obtain over Him the most [absolute] empire...

<summary>Saint-Martin argues that "predestination" is a misunderstanding; humans are simply returning to their original divine purpose. He describes God not as a distant judge, but as a responsive parent who reacts to human love and desire.</summary>

Yes, yes, it is a certain truth that if we so desired, we would govern God by our love, and that God grieves because we leave Him with so much authority, while He would wish only to employ toward us His compliance and most benevolent friendship.

# OF THE MAN-SPIRIT

All spiritual *sensitizations* <term>sensitizations: (original: *sensibilisations*) In Saint-Martin’s philosophy, these are the processes by which spiritual truths or the presence of God become perceptible to the soul’s internal senses, much as physical objects are felt by the body.</term>, which are but the productions of the operations of the Divinity, have the purpose of alerting the regions <note>In this context, "regions" likely refers to the various levels of existence or the faculties of the soul that might otherwise remain dormant.</note> that the Being exists, and that He is present; without this, they would forget Him, just as we would forget Him ourselves, because of His sublime existence. # THE MINISTRY

In this picture, we perceive how man proves God, and can be useful to God, since he must be His universal witness. We also see how dear this man must be to Him, because of this sublime destination. For as I have often explained, it is certain that if there were no God, we would no longer have anything to admire; but if there were no immortal spiritual soul, God would no longer have a permanent object that could be like the focus and the complete receptacle of His love.

Regarding the various names of man, as has already been seen, the first current name of man is *sorrow*, *affliction*: this name must resonate through our whole being before we can arrive at the gates of life and of the word <note>Original: *la parole*. In Saint-Martin's theology, the "Word" or "Speech" refers to the creative divine power that humans lost at the Fall and must recover through spiritual work.</note>. But the second name that man finds at the gates of life is *holiness* <note>Original: *sainteté*.</note>, whose Hebrew root signifies *to renew* <note>Saint-Martin likely refers to the concept of *Kadosh* (consecrated/set apart), interpreting it through a lens of spiritual restoration or being "made new" in the divine image.</note>. He will therefore give himself no rest until he has put himself in a state to be employed; for to be truly useful to the universal regions, it is not enough to reach a vivid and permanent feeling of one's title of spirit, if one does not furthermore succeed in being employed.

If we were to reflect on the labors <note>original: "les angoisses de la parole" — This refers to the spiritual "anguish" or the intense, sacrificial effort the divine Word undergoes to lower itself to the human level for the sake of our redemption.</note> of the Word, we would thank it for having the charitable generosity to devote itself, as it has done, to our rest; and we would devote ourselves to its rest, in our turn, just as it has devoted itself to ours.

It is by walking thus in these ways of love and charity that we would finally push back evil and pain from all regions, and that we would recognize in what immeasurable proportion good outweighs evil. For it is quite true that the demon is so wicked that, without the divine foundation or the goodness that has descended into man, we would not even be able to know that there is a God; but it is also true that men are so surrounded by this divine goodness that, without the wickedness of man, we would not even notice the existence of the demon.

There are even in the world such superb manifestations of the Word—and this independently of known traditions, and especially independently of the superb manifestation of nature—that when I cast my eyes upon the magnificent developments revealed by the generosity of Wisdom to some of its servants, I cannot help but be astonished by this prodigality on its part. I would be tempted to believe then that it <note>Referring to "Wisdom" (La Sagesse), often personified as Sophia in this tradition.</note> does not know the state of degradation, ignorance, and coarse hardening in which men find themselves regarding the progress of truth and the fertile reign of the spirit.

The habitual state of God and the spirits in relation to men is to believe them less evil than they are, because God and the spirits, dwelling in the abode of order, peace, virtue, and goodness, cast upon all that exists that tint of perfection which is their perpetual element. No matter how often they are deceived, in some way, by the repeated abuses of the human species, this does not prevent them from lavishing new favors upon it a moment later: a truth for which the two testaments of the Jews and the Christians <note>The Old and New Testaments of the Bible.</note> offer us an uninterrupted chain of testimonies; a truth that no longer surprises once one has a glimpse of the eternal generating root, which never ceases to continually renew itself.

This way of being on the part of God and the Spirits toward man does not at all oppose the continual vigilance they maintain regarding him to preserve, warn, and direct him in the paths that may be opened to him by wisdom, because all these things are works of love and beneficence, and that is their natural element.

# OF THE MAN-SPIRIT.

...will rising through this victim which is themselves, they might unite themselves to the holy desire and the sacred love of supreme wisdom, which seeks only to renew its ancient alliance or its original contract <note>The "original contract" refers to the state of grace and the relationship between God and humanity before the Fall.</note> with us.

<margin>69</margin>
It is thus that in celebrating the feast of the Sabbath, they ought to have risen in spirit above the six actions or elemental powers <note>These "six actions" represent the six days of creation or the material forces that govern the physical world.</note> which imprison man today, and unite their intimate being with the seven universal sources from which it flows, of which it is like a virtual representation, and from which it should never have been separated.

It is thus that the children of the new law, during the feast of the birth of the Repairer <term>The Repairer: (French: *le réparateur*) Saint-Martin’s title for Jesus Christ, who "repairs" the damage caused by the Fall of Man.</term>, ought, by your ministry and your example, to bring about the birth of this Repairer within themselves, and open the door for him to accomplish his entire mission within their own person, just as he accomplished it for the universality of mankind.

It is thus that at the feast of Passover <note>French: *Pâque*. This refers to both the Jewish Passover and the Christian Easter, signifying a "passing over" or resurrection.</note>, they ought to work to make him rise again within them from the tomb where our corrupted elements, our darkness, and our stains habitually keep him buried.

It is thus that at the feast of weeks <note>French: *fête des semaines*. This refers to Pentecost, occurring seven weeks after Passover, commemorating the descent of the Holy Spirit and the gift of tongues.</note> they ought to work to revive within themselves the understanding of all the languages that the spirit speaks ceaselessly to all men, and which our thick matter prevents us from hearing. Each year the return of each of these feasts should work in the faithful a new degree of development, and it is thus that they would progressively arrive at the goal of regeneration <term>Regeneration: The process of being spiritually reborn and restored to one's original divine nature.</term> which would be granted to them in this lowly world.

Yes, the man who constantly unites himself with his source <note>In Saint-Martin's thought, the "source" is the Divine or the "Universal Principle" from which man has fallen.</note> can reach such a point of activity and wisdom that his breath does not release a single puff that does not produce and spread glorious benefits, being like a quintessence of the universal purifying balm. <note>The "balm" is an alchemical metaphor for a restorative, healing spiritual substance that can repair the "corrosion" of the fallen world.</note>

Thus, man is a being unworthy of that name; he is an unjust being to the highest degree, a terrifying criminal, when he spends a single moment without spreading the active and holy word around him—whether upon nature, or upon man, or upon afflicted truth. <term>active word: "parole active." A central concept in this work, referring to speech that does not just describe things, but has the spiritual power to act upon and transform reality.</term>

Alas! Why is it possible—this terrifying, fruitless, and blind consumption of words that men engage in at every moment? The Psalmist <note>A reference to Psalm 5:9: "Their throat is an open sepulcher."</note> said that the mouth of man was an open sepulcher; but this earthly region, what then will it become, since it never ceases to receive into its womb these dead and cadaverous words that never cease to pour from the mouth of man, and which wander so freely in the atmosphere! What dark obscurity is that in which nearly the entire human family spends the whole length of its days!

They say that time is too short: alas! if they took the trouble to measure it, they would see its immense extent; they would be astonished by the abundance of time that God lavishes upon us. It is such that if we could employ an infinitely small part of the time given to us, we would soon be reinstated above time. <note>Saint-Martin believed that man’s original state was outside of linear time, and that spiritual work could return him to that "timeless" state.</note> Indeed, there is not a man who, in his life, has not had a moment sufficient to reach and embrace eternity; for there is not a single point in time in which this entire eternity, so to speak, is not enclosed.

> "If these somber pictures are not enough to awaken your pity and stimulate your glory, I will speak to you of him in whom resides the fullness of your divinity, of him in whom you have, as it were, deposited your own heart so that he might come to earth to transmit and distribute it to this same human family which had distanced itself from you."

# Manuscript Binding and Cover

The exterior of this volume is bound in decorative **marbled paper** using a "stone" or "shell" pattern. This design is composed of deep greens and blacks interspersed with small reddish-brown highlights. The spine and the adjacent narrow sections of the front and back covers are bound in light-colored **vellum** <term>a durable parchment made from animal skin</term>, which provides structural reinforcement.

A small, pale, rectangular label is affixed to the upper section of the spine. While there are faint traces of handwritten ink on the vellum, the text is largely illegible due to fading over time.
